title: At a Glance
use_cases: Use when developing genre-specific prompt patterns for Science Fiction, Romance, and Mystery.
Configure when setting up misdirection tables and clue plans to ensure fair-play mystery mechanics.
Implement when auditing character agency and relationship arcs to ensure earned HEA/HFN outcomes.
Use when pressure-testing world-building consequences to avoid static lore dumps.
Configure when using AI to explore scene variants while maintaining human-driven specificity and taste.
content:
- SF: one novum per scene; consequences over lore dumps.
- Romance: mutual agency, micro-repairs, earned HEA/HFN.
- Mystery: fair-play clues, misdirection tables.

AI can produce plausible genre beats fast—but plausibility is not freshness. Use it to explore alternatives, pressure-test stakes, and maintain continuity while you supply taste and specificity. Below are genre-by-genre prompt patterns and pitfalls to avoid. For deeper craft foundations, revisit AI templates, build consistency via daily AI habits, keep guardrails with AI ethics, test pacing in AI pacing, and stress-test continuity in AI continuity.

Freshness is one specific detail that changes how a familiar beat plays. Your job: find that detail. AI’s job: offer options so you can pick the best one.

“Create a fair-play clue plan: 7 clues with true meaning vs. false inference. Add one red herring per clue and place each by act.”

- Ask for 2 variants; pick one and compress.
- Table columns: Clue • False Inference • Real Meaning • Placement.

- Overstuffed subplots that blur motive and method.
- Villain monologues explaining everything.
- Last-minute reveals without seeded evidence.

Hook: A souvenir spoon appears in every crime‑scene photo online, but not in the evidence list. Turn: The spoon’s reflection reveals the real room layout.

“Map a relationship arc: Beat • Vulnerability • Boundary • Micro-Repair. Two variants: slow-burn vs. whirlwind. Ensure mutual agency.”

- Make careers and families create real schedule stakes.
- Seed small repairs after conflicts; avoid magic fixes.

- Unclear HEA/HFN terms relative to character goals.
- Conflicts solvable by a simple conversation.
- Agency asymmetry (one partner always yields).

Beat: First meet fails. Micro‑repair: One fixes the other’s bike chain in the rain; they laugh at the mess. Turn: New boundary—no secrets about work hours.

“List world logic: If [novum], then [3 consequences] at personal, societal, and environmental levels. Limit to 40 words per consequence.”

- Turn lore into obstacles and costs your character pays.
- One novum per scene; avoid stacking new tech every page.

- World rules that bend to solve the plot.
- Tech names as stakes (stakes must be human).
- Infodumps with no immediate consequence.

Novum: Memory backups at clinics. Consequence: People “restore” after arguments to erase guilt. Turn: Protagonist chooses not to restore, keeping pain—and growth.

“Design a chase sequence with three beats: obstacle • cost • information gained. Two variants: urban vs. rural.”

- Villains who act only to serve the plot.
- Endless action with no change in knowledge.

“List 5 everyday objects from this year/place and write a 120‑word scene where one object changes the choice at the end.”

- Long exposition without consequence.
- Modern attitudes pasted over period stakes.

For editorial conventions that influence reader expectations across genres, consult the Chicago Manual of Style. For research overviews on genre recognition and narrative modeling, literature surveys on arXiv provide useful context when designing guardrails and tests.

1. SF: List one novum and 3 consequences (personal, social, environmental). Place one consequence in a scene.
2. Romance: Write a micro‑repair after a disagreement (80–120 words). No grand speeches.
3. Mystery: Write a clue table with one honest clue that looks false. Draft the reveal line.

- Are the stakes personal and visible (not only global or abstract)?
- Can the reader spot one specific, fresh detail per scene?
- Does each scene change knowledge, status, or risk?

Lower on‑page violence; emphasize relationships and puzzle fairness. Seed clues early.

Keep banter crisp; build micro‑repairs after small mishaps; agency balanced.

One novum per scene; show consequences via action; avoid lecture paragraphs.

World notes are for you; scenes are for readers. Keep world notes short and move quickly to scenes where a choice costs the character something. Ask for two variants of a beat and choose the one with clearer consequences.

- SF ↔ Mystery: one novum creates fair‑play clues with new logic.
- Romance ↔ SF: relationship boundaries tested by tech limits.
- Mystery ↔ Romance: clue table + micro‑repairs after conflict.

No template sells a book alone. Use AI to explore options and keep continuity; rely on your taste for what feels true. Read your pages aloud. Ask two specific questions to a beta reader: “Where did you skim?” and “Which line made you curious?”

- SF: plain speech with one novel term at a time; explain by consequence.
- Romance: honest boundaries and small repairs; rhythm matters.
- Mystery: short, evasive lines that hide motive; reveal through slips.

1. Write a consequence of the novum that hurts the hero (SF).
2. Write a micro‑repair after a mishap (romance).
3. Write one clue that looks false but is true (mystery).

- SF: slow lore, fast consequences; one novum per scene.
- Romance: alternate tension and relief; show micro‑repairs.
- Mystery: slow build, fast reveals; seed clues early.

Open with a choice or a change the reader can see, not a paragraph of history. Add a concrete object and a sensory detail to ground the moment fast.

Crime stories may follow criminals or victims; detective stories follow an investigator. Decide which you’re writing. Then map tension accordingly—pursuit vs. deduction—and ask AI for two beat variants for the same premise.

- Cut any paragraph that explains what readers can learn by watching.
- Use objects readers can picture; avoid invented nouns until needed.
- Reveal one rule through a cost or obstacle.

- External: job, case, public harm, environment.
- Relational: trust, partnership, family, team.
- Personal: time, reputation, belonging, safety.

- Stakes are personal and visible; genre promises are satisfied.
- At least one fresh, specific detail per scene that fits the genre.
- Every scene changes knowledge, status, or risk for someone.
- Opening shows a change the reader can see (object + sensory anchor).

Use the checklist before each drafting session. A minute here saves hours of unfocused pages later—and helps you deliver the genre experience readers came for.

“Define one magic rule and three costs. Write a scene seed where the cost bites the hero.”

- Magic that solves every problem without cost.
- Endless lore before conflict.

“Build dread using the rule of three: normal • wrong • worse. Keep gore minimal; focus on sound and rhythm.”

- Describing what the character should be feeling instead of causing it with details.
- Shock without setup.
